segments.english: In the Yerushalmi, Shabbat, chapter Bemah Ishah, our Sages of blessed memory said: "'And the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.' Rabbi Reuven said: At that hour an angel came down and slapped that wicked one on his mouth, and said to him: 'Is your word right, and is there a son for him?' He returned and said: 'Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meishach and Abed-nego, who sent His angel and saved His servants.' 'His son' is not written here, but 'His angel.' Thus far." That is to say, Nebuchadnezzar the wicked thought that the angels are effects, descending in a chain of descent from him by nature, like a son from the father, according to the words of the Kabbalists concerning the sefirot of all the worlds, and likewise the souls; and for this the angel slapped him. And he returned and said: 'who sent His angel, etc.' Here you have it explicit, coming out of the words of Midrash Rabbah and the Yerushalmi, contrary to the words of the Kabbalists. And all that exists, the Holy One, blessed be He, brought into being in His kindness, something from nothing, from the first form down to a small gnat; and not that they are drawn from His essence, as the son comes into being by the power of the seed drawn from his father.

tokens.note: פ' = פרק: chapter.

Aramaic: the appearance of the fourth figure in Dan 3:25 (וריויה, 'and the appearance').
Aramaic bar elahin: 'son of the gods' (Dan 3:25).
ר' = Rabbi.
סטר: to slap.
רשיעא: the wicked one, Nebuchadnezzar, named at 2:10.55.
תקין: right, correct (Aramaic).
The blessing is Dan 3:28 (Aramaic), in the Yerushalmi's wording.
אלההון: Aramaic 'their God'. The suffix is redundant before 'די שדרך מישך ועביד נגו' ('of Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego'), so Dan 3:28 is read 'the God of Shadrach …'; the English does the same.
בריה: 'son'. The Yerushalmi says the verse writes 'angel' here, not 'son'.
ע"כ: 'thus far', closing the Yerushalmi quotation.
ור"ל: 'that is to say' (רוצה לומר). From here the author speaks in his own voice.
Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, of Dan 3.
עלולים: effects, the things caused (עלה / עלול, cause and effect).

grammar: The Yerushalmi is quoted as the author's source, and its Aramaic is translated as he gives it. Dan 3:25 and 3:28 are quoted inside it, in single quotation marks.
'ע"כ' (2:10.53) closes the Yerushalmi quotation. From 2:10.54 the author argues in his own voice, and his argument turns on the words 'בר' (son) and 'מלאכיה' (his angel).
'ובר אית ליה?' is an Aramaic question, 'and is there a son for him?'. 'סטרו' (2:10.21, 2:10.76) is a verb of the angel's action, 'slapped him'.

'ולא שהם נמשכים' (2:10.107-109) is 'and not that they are drawn': the negative ולא rejects the Kabbalists' claim that the angels and all things are drawn from His essence like a son from the seed. 'ושכל' (2:10.95) opens with ש, 'that'.
segments.note: The Yerushalmi passage is the author's source. The argument of the paragraph is set by 2:10.54 onward, where the author draws his conclusion from it against the Kabbalists.
apparatus: Dan 3:25 (Aramaic): the Yerushalmi's wording 'וריויה די רביעאה דמי לבר אלהין' is kept; 'son of the gods' is the verse's phrase.
Dan 3:28 (Aramaic): the blessing of the three men, with 'בריה' contrasted with 'מלאכיה' as the Yerushalmi gives them.
Yerushalmi: tractate and chapter as the author gives them (Shabbat, 'Bemah Ishah'); no folio or halakhah number is added.
Q2 (Wikisource additions): the base text is translated; no word is flagged until the 1931 scan is collated.
context: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had Shadrach, Meishach and Abed-nego thrown into a furnace (Dan 3), and called the fourth figure he saw there 'like a son of the gods' (Dan 3:25). In the Yerushalmi's story an angel strikes him for it. The author quotes it against the Kabbalists' claim that the angels descend from God as a son from a father.

segments.english: The conclusion from all this is that no face or form is to be worshipped of all the created things that exist in the upper and the lower world, which the Name, may He be blessed, brought into being in His kindness. For to Him alone it is fitting to worship and to pray, and for this the commandment and the warning came at Sinai: "I am the LORD your God. You shall have no other gods," as the Rambam of blessed memory wrote in chapter two of the Laws of Idolatry. And in chapter three of the Laws of Repentance he wrote, and these are his words: "And these are those who have no share in the world to come, but are cut off and perish for the greatness of their wickedness and their sins, forever and ever: the heretics and the apikorsim, etc." And in the law that follows it he wrote: "Five are those that are called heretics. The one who says that there is no God, and no ruler of the world, and the one who says that there is a ruler, but they are two or more, and the one who says that there is one Lord, but He is a body and possessed of a form, and the one who says that He is not alone the first and the rock of all. Likewise one who worships one other than Him in order to be an intercessor between him and the Lord of the worlds. Each of these five is a heretic. Thus far." And the Rav Lechem Mishneh wrote on the fourth division that our Master wrote, "and the one who says that He is not alone the first, etc." The Ravad wrote: "like one who said, your God is a great painter, but He found for Himself great pigments, formlessness and void, and darkness and water and wind, and with them made what He made." Thus far, the words of the Ravad. And the Rav Lechem Mishneh explains that his intention is to add to the words of our Master that although he concedes that no cause preceded our God, for whose sake He came to be, but says that He created the world something from something, then this one is a heretic; see there. In our case, the belief of the new Kabbalah, as explained in their books, according to our understanding and the understanding of many great ones, wise of heart, among our Rabbis who separated from it, early and late, like the Ribash and Chavot Yair, cited in Pitchei Teshuvah and the other later authorities: in it have gathered and come three or four of these words that our Rabbis said, that whoever believes thus has no share in the world to come. First, a multiplicity of divinities: Ein Sof, and Adam Kadma'ah, and Adam Kadmon, and Atik, and Arikh Anpin, and Abba and Imma, and Ze'ir and his Nukva! Second, that they have a subtle body, namely light, and Ein Sof is a soul to these bodies. Third, that the worship is not to the First Cause, which they call Ein Sof, but to Ze'ir Anpin, which is the last cause among these causes. Fourth, that he is an intermediary drawing down the flow from those upper attributes, which are Atik, Arikh Anpin, Abba and Imma, and they call him son of Abba and Imma, and he is also father to the Keter of Creation, according to the chain of descent of the worlds, in their opinion, the Merciful One save us.

tokens.note: המורם: the conclusion, what is inferred from what precedes.
פרצוף: 'face', in the generic sense (not the Kabbalistic partzuf).
צורה: form.

ה' = the Tetragrammaton, read as 'the LORD' in the verse.
Exod 20:2-3 is cut short by the author after 'אחרים': the English gives only what is written (no 'who brought you out …', no 'before Me'). See `apparatus`.
שכ' = שכתב: 'wrote'.
הרמב"ם: the Rambam (Moses Maimonides).
ז"ל: 'of blessed memory'.
ע"ז: Avodah Zarah, 'strange worship'. Here the Laws of Idolatry of the Mishneh Torah.
Hilchot Teshuvah: the Laws of Repentance of the Mishneh Torah.
וז"ל: 'and these are his words'.
המינין: the heretics (singular min).
האפיקורסין: the apikorsim (singular apikoros), as the decisions fix it ('apikoros'); a heretic of another kind than the מינים before them.
וכו': 'etc.'. The quotation is cut short.
כ': 'wrote' (כתב).
שם: 'there' in the existential 'שאין שם' ('that there is no … there'), not 'name' and not 'any'.
מנהיג: ruler, governor.
שם: 'there', as at 2:11.80.
שם: 'there', as at 2:11.80.
תמונה: a visible form.
לזולתו: 'other than Him'; the suffix refers to God.
מליץ: intercessor.
ע"כ: 'thus far', closing the Rambam's quotation.
הרב: 'the Rav'; the English keeps it ('the Rav Lechem Mishneh'), as 'the Rav Mikdash Melekh' in the decisions. The Lechem Mishneh is the commentary on the Mishneh Torah; the author of it is meant.
רבינו: 'our Master', the Rambam.
וכו': 'etc.'.
הראב"ד: the Ravad (Rabad), whose criticisms of the Mishneh Torah the Lechem Mishneh cites.
תהו ובהו: Gen 1:2, 'formless and void'. The Ravad's list takes them as materials, so 'formlessness and void'.
עכ"ל: 'thus far, the words of', closing the Ravad's quotation.
לח"מ: the Lechem Mishneh.
רבי': 'our Master' (the Rambam).
יש מיש: 'something from something' (the phrase is translated, not transliterated; decisions, wave 1). The Lechem Mishneh's point: creation from a prior matter.
ע"ש: 'see there' (עיין שם).
דידן: 'ours'; 'in our case'.
הקבלה: the Kabbalah. The author's term is 'the new Kabbalah'.
לב: 'heart'; 'wise of heart'.
הריב"ש: the Ribash.
חו"י: read as Chavot Yair, the fixed spelling of the decisions. The expansion is not certain.
פתחי תשובה: Pitchei Teshuvah, a commentary on the Shulchan Arukh.
נקבצו באו בה: the subject is 'תלת וארבע מלי' (2:11.221-223), 'three or four words'; see `readings` for the other parse.
בה: 'in it', the belief of the new Kabbalah (2:11.193-195).
לעה"ב: le-olam ha-ba, 'the world to come'.
א"ס: Ein Sof, literally 'without end'. This is the first occurrence in the unit.
קדמאה: Adam Kadma'ah, a distinct entity from Adam Kadmon.
קדמון: Adam Kadmon, 'Primordial Man'.
עתיק: Atik, literally 'Ancient', a partzuf.
אריך אנפין: Arikh Anpin, 'Long Face'.
אבא: Abba, 'Father'.
אימא: Imma, 'Mother'.
זעיר: Ze'ir Anpin, 'Small Face'.
נוקביה: his Nukva, 'female'.
נשמה: soul.
לז"א: Ze'ir Anpin, 'small face'.
לאו"א: 'Abba and Imma'. The author argues from the name, 'son of Abba and Imma'.
כתר: Keter, the crown.
דבריאה: 'of Creation', Beriah, the second of the four worlds (Emanation, Creation, Formation, Making); the decisions translate the names of the four worlds.
רחמנא ליצלן: 'the Merciful One save us', the formula kept, with its irony.

grammar: The Rambam's words run from 2:11.51 ('וז"ל') to 2:11.125 ('ע"כ'). They are cut short at 'וכו'' (2:11.70); 'ובדין שאחריו כ'' (2:11.71-73) is the author's link, so the quotation marks close and open again around it. The author's gloss starts at 2:11.126.
'כ'' (2:11.73, 2:11.140) is 'wrote', an abbreviation of כתב; 'שכ'' (2:11.39) is 'that wrote'. 'הרב' (2:11.127, 2:11.165) is a word of the text, 'the Rav', before the book's name.
'שאין לעבוד' (2:11.4-5) is 'that one must not worship': 'לעבוד' is the verb 'to worship', used of God throughout the paragraph.
'שם' in 'שאין שם אלוה' (2:11.79-81), 'שיש שם מנהיג' (2:11.86-88) and 'שיש שם רבון' (2:11.95-97) is the adverb 'there' of the existential 'there is', not 'name'.

In the long sentence at 2:11.191-232 the subject of 'נקבצו באו' (2:11.218-219) is 'תלת וארבע מלי' (2:11.221-223), 'three or four words'; 'בה' is 'in it', the belief of the new Kabbalah. The words between ('כפי המבואר … ושאר אחרונים') say by whose understanding. 'דאמור רבנן' is Aramaic: 'that the Rabbis said'.
'חדא', 'שנית', 'שלישית', 'רביעית' (2:11.233, 248, 259, 275) number the four 'words'. The first is a noun phrase (רבוי האלוהות); the others open with שהם, שהעבודה, שהוא.
segments.note: The paragraph is the author's conclusion from the Rambam's law (the Rambam, the Lechem Mishneh and the Ravad are quoted), followed by the four 'words' of the Rabbis that he finds in the new Kabbalah.
apparatus: Exod 20:2-3: the author quotes 'אנכי ה' אלהיך לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים', leaving out 'who brought you out of the land of Egypt …' (v. 2) and 'על פני' (v. 3); the English follows his wording, without 'before Me'.
Rambam, Laws of Idolatry ch. 2 and Laws of Repentance ch. 3 (Mishneh Torah), as the author gives them; no halakhah number is added. The Rambam's quotation is cut short at 'וכו'' (2:11.70).

Gen 1:2: 'תהו ובהו וחשך ומים ורוח' in the Ravad's words echoes the verse ('formless and void, and darkness … and the wind (or spirit) of God … the waters'); here the words are the painter's materials, so 'formlessness and void' and 'wind'.
The Lechem Mishneh and the Ravad are quoted as the author gives them; 'וכו'' is kept as 'etc.'.
יש מיש: 'something from something', translated, not transliterated (decisions, wave 1: יש מאין / יש מיש).
חו"י: the expansion Chavot Yair (the fixed spelling in the decisions) is a reading, not a certainty.
שם (2:11.80, 87, 96) is 'there'; 'name' is not possible in the grammar of 'שיש שם'.
context: The Mishneh Torah is the Rambam's code of Jewish law; the Laws of Idolatry and the Laws of Repentance are two of its sections, as cited here.
The Lechem Mishneh is a commentary on the Mishneh Torah. Pitchei Teshuvah is a commentary on the Shulchan Arukh.

readings.english: the authorities gathered and came against it: three or four of these words that our Rabbis said, "Whoever believes thus has no share in the world to come."
readings.note: The reading of the draft, which makes the Ribash, Chavot Yair and the later authorities the subject and בה 'against it'; the English chosen takes 'three or four words' as the subject and בה as 'in it'.
